To:  Joint Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology From: Andrew Blunt, Sierra Club Maine Date:  April 22, 2025 Re:  Testimony in Support of L.D. 1700: An Act to Create a Direct Investment Pilot Project Under the Maine Clean Energy and Sustainability Accelerator __________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
Dear Senator Lawrence, Representative Sachs, and Members of the Joint Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology,
I write on behalf of the Sierra Club Maine Chapter, representing over 22,000 supporters and members statewide. Founded in 1892, Sierra Club is one of our nation's oldest and largest environmental organizations. We work diligently to amplify the power of our 3.8 million members nationwide as we work towards combating climate change and promoting a just and sustainable economy. To that end, we urge you to vote "Ought to Pass" on L.D. 1700.
L.D. 1700 builds on the creation of the Maine Clean Energy and Sustainability Accelerator (the "Accelerator"), as it was passed in the 130th Legislature. It clarifies the ability of the Accelerator to provide direct investment services to clean energy projects and battery storage. The bill also compels the Efficiency Maine Trust (or "the Trust") to allocate $1 million in existing funding to pilot this type of direct investment, either through low-interest loans or equity, directing the Trust to explore its role as a direct investor.
So far, through programs like Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE), the Trust has been hugely successful providing low-interest loans to commercial property owners through the Accelerator. What L.D. 1700 seeks is to explore the role that the Trust can play providing low-cost capital directly towards the development of renewable energy generation or battery storage.
State agency, municipal, and private energy renewable energy projects have complex and diverse financing needs. The Accelerator is in a unique position to participate as a flexible investor in Maine's clean energy economy. Through this program, the Trust can provide competitive, low-cost, and low-risk capital to developers, and can spend public money to fill critical financial gaps for developers. For a project struggling to secure capital, that type of targeted intervention can make a huge difference in whether or not it ultimately gets built. The program as written will have flexible investment criteria as well, allowing the Trust to target municipal energy projects, grid resiliency projects, or other private or publicly owned renewable or energy storage projects depending on need, and where public capital is likely to make the largest difference.
Overall, L.D. 1700 encourages the Trust to invest its funds directly into our economy and create clean energy jobs for Maine people. The Sierra Club strongly supported the establishment of the

 Accelerator, and, through projects like the one created in this bill, we're excited to support its growth as a substantial financial actor in our clean energy transition.
For the above reasons, we urge an `Ought to Pass' vote on L.D. 1700.
Sincerely,
Andrew Blunt Sierra Club Maine Chapter Legislative and Political Strategist

Testimony of Chirag Lala to the Joint Standing Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology in support of LD 1700 An Act to Create a Direct Investment Pilot Project Under the Clean Energy and Sustainability Accelerator
April 23, 2025
Senator Lawrence, and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology of the Maine State Legislature,
My name is Chirag Lala and I am the Director of Energy at the Center for Public Enterprise. I am submitting this written testimony in support of LD 1700.
The bill instructs Efficiency Maine Trust (EMT) to provide capital to qualified projects in the form of debt financing credit enhancements; aggregation and warehousing, equity capital, including co-investments; leases; loans; and other financial products approved by the EMT board. This would be undertaken as part of a two-year pilot program (hereafter referred to in this testimony as the EMT Pilot) via the Maine Clean Energy and Sustainability Accelerator and would see EMT utilize no less than $1 million to provide capital. The EMT Green Bank offers a number of financing programs already, including a C-PACE Program, home energy loans, small business energy loans, loans to participants in the Manufactured (Mobile) Home Initiative to facilitate a switch to whole-home heat pump systems, a municipal lease program, and targeted loan offerings to long-term care facilities. However, EMT does not currently offer direct financing to developers of clean energy and storage projects despite having the authority to do so. That is what LD 1700 proposes to change.
Energy projects are typically not financed with one source of financing. Their financing is often described as a "capital stack," a mix of different financing arrangements whose capital cost and terms vary considerably. If more expensive sources of financing (whether debt or equity) can be replaced by cheaper sources of financing, the project's overall capital cost (the weighted average cost of capital or WACC) will decrease and it will be easier for investment to proceed. Similarly, if public sources of financing provide capital that is otherwise difficult to procure at any price (such as construction financing), then investment will also be made more likely to succeed. Providing patient and cost effective financing, even if only for a portion of project capital stacks, is the premise behind most public sector financing programs. Cheaper and more patient financing allows a project to undertake investment knowing that a smaller portion of its subsequent revenues will be required to cover debt servicing. (See Figure 1 in the Appendix for an illustration of the capital stack concept.)
Several state and local green banks and financing institutions provide comparable services. Examples are provided below:
 The Connecticut Green Bank provided subordinated debt as part of its early solar leasing programs.1

Executive Summary
Revolving Loan Funds (RLFs) allow governments to speed up and reduce the costs of socially important investments by providing critical pieces of finance that private capital markets are unable to supply at an acceptable rate, while receiving sufficient enough returns to be self-sustaining. RLFs have a crucial role to play in accelerating the energy transition and catalyzing the potential of the Inflation Reduction Acts (IRAs) provisions to enable a greater public role in the energy sector.
In this report, the Center for Public Enterprise (CPE) illustrates the operations and functions of RLFs more generally and explains how they can play a key role in the development of clean energy. We zero in on how states, municipalities, and instrumentalities can use RLF as part of a broader strategy to mobilize IRA resources such as elective pay and loans from federal agencies such as the Department of Energy. Finally, we provide case studies of successful RLFs from very different contexts to illustrate the different strategies that RLFs can pursue and draw conclusions about where they have potential in the clean energy sector and what further steps need to be taken to maximize their impact.

I. Introduction
Elective pay provides the United States' tax incentives for clean energy development to public power developers, whose lower break-evens allow them to take more risks on energy deployment. Through elective pay, nonprofit and public entities without a tax bill to speak of can receive tax credit disbursements in the form of a direct payment from the IRS. However, elective pay, which can only cover between 30 to 50 percent of a project's capital costs, cannot on its own galvanize the full potential of public power.1 Public developers will therefore also require additional sources of longer-term, low-cost capital that private market participants may not be in a position to provide. Moreover, elective payments from the IRS take time to process, and they are only issued after a project is operational. This means that elective pay-eligible projects need construction financing to cover costs and payments between when a project enters development and when its developer receives an elective payment from the IRS.
Construction financing is available from private lenders, but it can be expensive--especially as interest rates have risen. This loss of liquidity means that spreads on construction loans for new projects have climbed around 350 basis points (3.5%) above the benchmark secured overnight financing rate (SOFR) since late 2023.2 Tight construction finance conditions will blunt the effect of any tax credits. If projects do not secure sufficient upfront financing, capital expenditure will not proceed and tax credits will not be disbursed. These financial conditions especially impact public and nonprofit developers using elective pay. Private developers can sell their tax credits to third parties with large tax bills and free cash--typically large banks--which can provide developers upfront financing at a discount relative to the amount of the tax credit. Critically, this means that both tax equity partners and credit purchasers on transfer markets can finance a project quickly--usually near the end of its construction period, speeding the rollover of costly, short-term construction debt to less expensive, long-term permanent debt. Private developers can secure cash for their tax credits while public entities are waiting for the IRS to approve and process tax credits. Project developers can thus use the proceeds of the monetized tax credits to pay off construction debts.3 Developers preparing elective pay-eligible projects may therefore face construction loans with longer terms and higher interest rates.
Fortunately, states and municipalities have developed policy tools appropriate to solving such a financing challenge: revolving loan funds (RLFs). RLFs allow

RLFs are thus ideal instruments for short-term positions in project capital stacks, particularly to fill bridge and pre-development financing needs. Reducing these short-term, upfront costs also potentially allows a project developer to refinance the project in different, longer-term markets at a lower rate than it would without RLF's participation.4 This means that short-term investments by the public not only pay for themselves but reduce overall development costs, and bring projects that otherwise might never be built to completion.
This issue brief will describe the basic operations of RLFs, pathways for governments to establish them, and the ingredients that make them successful. We then examine how an RLF can be utilized to facilitate the use of the IRA's elective pay tax credits.
II. What are revolving loan funds?
A revolving loan fund (RLF) is an investment fund that makes loans to projects which, at a later date, return the principal and interest to the revolving fund.5 Returned funds are then recycled, making loans to other projects. As the Department of Energy puts it, "RLFs can be `evergreen' sources of capital that are recycled over and over again to fund projects well into the future" as long as default rates remain low6
RLFs generally aim to recycle capital quickly. Their short durations make them an ideal tool to finance upfront capital expenditures, which developers can refinance at a lower rate and longer term as projects reach completion and its revenues become more certain.By covering upfront installation and construction costs--construction being the riskiest period of project development--an RLF allows developers to reach a point where they can borrow against installed assets with predictable cash flows to pay off the RLF's construction loan, effectively refinancing the RLF.
A relatively simple model for an energy RLF transaction takes five steps:
1. Capitalization: A financial entity, such as a state investment authority, green bank, or a public developer, sets up an RLF to provide bridge loans for the construction of an energy asset. The RLF can be financed by grants, appropriations, windfalls, tax revenues, or other sources of public funds.

2. Lending: The RLF issues loans to developers that need pre-development or construction financing. These loans can cover some or all of the bridge or construction-period capital stack.
3. Operation: The project developer builds the asset using the RLF's loan (and, if applicable, supplementary sources of bridge financing such as down payments or other loans).
4. Refinancing: As the project nears operation, the developer searches for new, longer-term financing to pay off the RLF loan. Examples of refinancing sources for clean energy projects include tax credits and long-term energy off-take contracts from future customers, usually known as power purchase agreements (PPAs).7 The RLF can facilitate this refinancing operation by providing the term loan itself, through the use of a capital fund that is separated from its main balance sheet--though it need not do so if alternative refinancing options are made available to the developer by other lenders.8
5. Revolving: The replenished RLF provides bridge financing to a new project, restarting the cycle.
With its return on investment recouped in step 3, the RLF can lend to additional projects in step 5. This process is depicted in Figure 1 below. (For a T-Chart depiction of an RLF, see the Appendix.) Over time, RLFs can grow from the debt service payments they earn. That growth is slow--but fast balance sheet growth isn't the goal. Rather, a successful RLF's main aim is to revolve as quickly as possible to ensure as many new projects as possible get built; achieving this goal requires taking on risks to finance projects that either fail to secure private bridge financing or to substitute for more expensive sources of bridge financing. Any critical energy project that cannot get built thanks to inadequate financing is a policy failure; RLFs help policymakers avoid this outcome.
A developer can often pair an RLF with another piece of longer-term financing funded by a private sector partner, or a public entity with a longer investment horizon, at the outset of project development. For example, public authorities in states with Commercial Property Assessment Clean Energy (C-PACE) programs can use an RLF to originate loans for commercial building energy retrofits against the promise of

III. Establishing an RLF
Public authorities at any level of government are well-placed to seed RLFs or complementary capital funds if they have spare cash from windfall revenues or federal grants on hand. Public authorities could use their balance sheets as the revolving fund--channeling asset income into new loans--or, in more complex arrangements, set up an external, off-balance-sheet financial entity, likely a special purpose vehicle (SPV), to do the same.10
An RLF should not be understood as a traditional one-time expenditure like a grant. That is, money spent seeding an RLF does not go away; RLFs earn a return on their investment while recycling capital repeatedly to execute their main mission: bringing multiple projects to the finish line.11 Because an RLF loan retains its value, so long as it is repaid, it remains as an essential source of support for new projects. RLFs are, therefore, an ideal place for governments to park windfall revenues, or rents from publicly owned assets such as land and natural resources, and to invest those revenues into projects that target long-term social outcomes--particularly if governments have extra revenue that they would otherwise forgo if they do not spend it by the end of their fiscal year. Governments contemplating how to utilize unexpected budget windfalls and manage income sources--including grants for investment, federal fiscal assistance (for example, one-time pandemic relief funds disbursed to local and state governments), and philanthropic contributions--should seriously consider seeding or expanding RLFs that advance their desired outcomes.12 It is better to recycle these limited funding sources than deploy them only once.13
Once RLFs are established, whether by grants or bonds, they do not necessarily need to rely on further appropriations to continue functioning. However, one-time

V. Enabling elective pay with RLF lending
The Inflation Reduction Act's elective pay provisions make it significantly easier for policymakers to set up financially sustainable revolving funds specifically designed to support publicly owned and non-profit clean energy developers.17 An RLF used to provide construction financing to elective pay-eligible projects could revolve as soon as the IRS issues an elective payment to the project developer.
A revolving fund structure for an elective pay-eligible project might work like this:
1. A financial entity, such as a state investment authority, green bank, or a public developer itself, provides bridge financing from its RLF to a public or nonprofit energy developer, for the construction of a clean energy-generating asset.
2. The project developer builds the asset, makes an elective pay election, places the project in service, and earns revenue.18 After the project is placed in service, the developer receives an elective payment from the IRS. (Let us assume that this elective payment is for the investment tax credit, or ITC, which covers between 30-50 percent of the project's capital expenditures.)
3. The developer uses a combination of elective payment and revenue (from wholesale market revenues, rate payments, or PPA revenue) to buy out and refinance the RLF's construction bridge debt.
4. The funds are returned to the RLF, which can make further loans to new projects.
This structure implies that the RLF is a public lender with capital enough to provide bridge financing (Ingredient 1), and that it is lending to project developers whose projects have cash flow from energy savings, electricity sales, and elective payment (Ingredients 3, 4, 5). It is not implied that this RLF has additional financing to fill a project's entire capital (Ingredient 2) stack, or that the RLF can refinance its position in a project (Ingredient 6). VI. A successful pedigree
This section highlights three example revolving loan fund programs, from Texas, Maine, and New Mexico. The structure of each program is similar in design--but each RLF targets very different goals. Policymakers should treat these examples as models for the kind of programs they can design to support energy investments.
The Texas Permanent School Fund
The Texas Permanent School Fund (TPSF) is a state sovereign wealth fund, which is seeded by revenues generated from royalties on the sales of grazing, mineral prospecting, and oil and gas development rights on publicly owned lands.21 The TPSF takes the income streams from these royalties and acquires long-term capital market assets and other equities. The interest and dividends earned on these assets and equities is transferred to Texas' school districts. The TPSF, which stands outside Texas's traditional budget process, is technically self-financing. The majority of the Fund's revenues are disbursed as direct cash payments to the school districts based on a proportion of their daily school attendance.
Notably, the TPSF also runs an implicit RLF through its Bond Guarantee Program (BGP). The BGP allows school districts with credit ratings below AAA to have their debt guaranteed at the Permanent School Fund's AAA rating (which is itself backed by the TPSF's assets), thereby lowering their cost of borrowing on the municipal bond market. Borrowers are given an effective loan guarantee from the state: if the district defaults, the state will cover its remaining payments to creditors.
The BGP functions as seed capital for projects (Ingredient 1). The TPSF allows the school district to issue bonds for their entire school construction capital stacks at a lower interest rate than their credit rating would otherwise imply (ingredients 1 and 2). The district then acts as a developer and makes capital investments in new projects, such as building and repairing school facilities or funding new educational programs (ingredients 3 and 4), which are paid back out of tax revenues (ingredient 5). Thanks to the bond's higher credit rating, school district residents have lower tax burdens relative to the alternative where their district cannot access TPSF leverage. An additional source of revenue for the school district is the potential long-run savings from the projects it develops. Greater savings raise the relative value of the district's tax revenue

The BGP is an implicit RLF because there is no source of capital that is actively revolving; rather, the TPSF reassigns its capital to new guarantees as old school bond issuances are paid off. The BGP constitutes a mechanism for smooth and steady borrowing for a vital public need: education. This is a mechanism that would not otherwise exist without the TPSF's balance sheet, its revenues, and its credit rating. Since the guarantee program began in 1983, it has not seen a single default. This is because, like most successful RLFs, the BGP conducts extensive due diligence on its applicants and requires an upfront $1,500 processing fee to cover these costs.
The Clean Water and Drinking Water State Revolving Funds
The Environmental Protection Agency has run the Clean Water and Drinking Water State Revolving Loan Fund programs (known as the SRFs; CWSRF and DWSRF, respectively), since 1987. Congress massively recapitalized both through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. These federal appropriations are provided as grants to state governments, which must use them to capitalize and administer revolving funds for eligible water-related infrastructure projects. The federal government sets eligibility criteria; state governments administer funds and run the loan programs.
States have the authority to make concessional loans, refinance or guarantee municipalities' project debts, and borrow against their capitalization to make additional loans. Insofar as the federal government expects states to keep their SRFs solvent, SRFs are expected to use revenues from the principal and interest repayments of individual projects to back new loans and guarantees to subsequent projects. States can run their SRFs through their own financing instrumentalities, such as bond banks, and set their own project eligibility and loan issuance criteria.
The Maine Municipal Bond Bank, for example, runs the state's CWSRF program: it receives financing from the federal government (Ingredient 1), which it blends with its own financing (Ingredient 2). The Bond Bank has its own set of eligible project developers (Ingredient 3), usually municipalities, that it lends to for eligible water management projects (Ingredient 4). The Bond Bank ensures that eligible borrowers are able to repay over the term of their loans (Ingredient 5) and, if the borrower does not default, the loan principal and interest are repaid (Ingredient 6).

New Mexico Finance Authority's Public Project Revolving Fund
The New Mexico Finance Authority (NMFA) is a state financing instrumentality created in 1992 to finance infrastructure projects for local governments and state departments (Ingredient 3, 4). Its flagship program is the Public Project Revolving Fund (PPRF). The PPRF provides both market- and subsidized-loans (Ingredient 1) to projects including roadworks, water system upgrades, public buildings, hospitals and other healthcare facilities, utilities, and other similar facilities.
The Finance Authority replenishes its RLF by issuing tax-exempt bonds (Ingredient 6). Project income (Ingredient 5) repays the NMFA, which in turn redirects those payments to repaying proceeds on the tax-exempt bonds. The NMFA's borrowing capacity and credit rating are maintained at AAA due to its diverse range of borrowers and annual transfers to the NMFA from New Mexico's Governmental Gross Receipts Tax. In turn, local and state governments are able to finance capital projects more cheaply.
VII. A public development revolution
RLFs offer states, municipalities, and their instrumentalities a powerful tool with which to catalyze new development. RLFs break down the financial barriers that many developers face when they wish to engage in new projects. This is especially the case for public-interest projects, which often face additional hurdles to securing financing

Even more ambitiously, RLFs can allow state entities to leverage public funding sources to finance projects that the private sector cannot. The passage of the IRA has opened the window for a new wave of public energy development, particularly for clean energy.
However, establishing RLFs requires governments to rethink their relationship to capital markets and the broader process of project development. Governments must first identify their points of leverage: how does their position as public entities create opportunities for tax and financing support, and what unique resources do they have that they can tap as revenue streams? Policymakers should also familiarize themselves with the idiosyncratic project development processes specific to critical sectors, and how investments in each are financed across their many phases. This way, they will be able to identify granular financing bottlenecks that they can resolve through infusions of cheaper, patient public capital. Achieving this goal will require building the internal underwriting and community engagement capacity required to identify investment gaps and local needs, conduct due diligence on developers, and, if needed, initiate the project development process themselves. But the benefits are worth it!
An important caveat is this: many successful RLFs operate in well-established, relatively deep markets, like in municipal and school finance. The existing liquidity in those markets allows public developers to easily find co-lenders and longer-term capital market investors who want to refinance RLFs' lending (Ingredients 2, 6). But the efficiencies of these markets are not a "natural" result of capitalism: they are a policy outcome.24 Water finance is heavily backstopped by the federal government's water finance instrumentalities, and school bonds are legally tax-exempt at state and federal levels, too.25 Federal interventions could further develop secondary markets for debt from renewable and clean energy projects, and recent public investments in infrastructure and energy offer new opportunities to augment or create RLF programs with these secondary market facilities.
The good news is that even the process of setting up an RLF can, over time, help governments develop and deepen their knowledge and capacity. The more the RLF

One way to do this is for RLFs to work with other federal and state agencies to provide other ingredients necessary to their success. A public developer can commit to projects for the RLF to fund; public power agencies or community aggregators can provide a ready off-taker or income source to RLF projects; and additional public capital can be set aside to ensure public projects can access longer term financing. Just because an RLF only requires the initial seed capital does not mean governments have to rely solely on the private sector to provide those other ingredients.

Through operating RLFs, their administrators develop the soft skills and coordination mechanisms necessary for executing successful development policies and meeting legislative priorities. The more RLF administrators learn and take on, the more capable the public sector becomes, and the more capacity governments have to directly tackle economic development objectives. Senator Lawrence, Representative Sachs, and honorable members of the Energy Utilities and Technology Committee:
My name is Rachel Ackoff. On behalf of the 32,000 members of Maine People's Alliance, I am pleased to submit testimony in support of LD 1700 - An Act to Create a Direct Investment Pilot Project Under the Maine Clean Energy and Sustainability Accelerator.
The members of Maine People's Alliance would be thrilled to have Efficiency Maine invest existing funds in State or municipal energy projects, resiliency projects, or other private or publicly owned renewable or energy storage projects like an energy storage facilitate or solar for schools or municipal buildings across Maine. EMT's investments will help reduce costs associated with renewable energy projects, but even more important to our members, it will also bring benefits to the people of Maine. EMT as a partial owner of a project means that a portion of the projects' profits would go back to EMT and could be used for the benefit of all Mainers. If this bill passes, the state can earn money from the loans and equity stakes it takes. As Maine recoups our initial investments, Maine can establish a "revolving fund" to quickly invest in renewable and storage projects even with a limited amount of funds.
At the local level, our members also stand to gain from EMT's investment in on-site renewal energy projects that will improve power quality and the reliability of electrical supply.
In conclusion, I urge you to vote ought to pass on LD 1700 - An Act to Create a Direct Investment Pilot Project Under the Maine Clean Energy and Sustainability Accelerator. This legislation will benefit the state, energy ratepayers, and our children whose future hangs in the balance as we make this clean energy transition.
Thank you for your attention to this matter.
